schema.problem: Tactile images are sensor- and physics-specific, so effective network architectures often require expert intuition and extensive manual iteration; existing neural architecture search can reduce this burden but is computationally expensive and restricted to hand-designed search spaces, limiting architectural novelty and diversity.
schema.motivation: Automating tactile perception architecture discovery would lower the cost of adapting networks to new sensors and tasks, and large language models now make code-level architectural mutation and diversity-driven evolution practical.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses a large language model to generate code-level mutations and crossovers of network architectures, combined with a MAP-Elites quality-diversity loop that preserves diverse elite architectures while preferentially reusing prompts that consistently yield improvements. Exploration is steered by two behavioural descriptors covering structural variation and compute-size trade-offs. The method is applied to vision-based tactile force regression and grating classification.
schema.research_plan: (1) The framework is run on tactile force regression and grating classification, measuring the proportion of generated architectures that are trainable and the best validation fitness across generations; support requires high trainable yield and improving fitness. (2) A post-search high-fidelity evaluation compares the final architectures with an expert baseline on force prediction and fine-grained grating classification; support is matching or exceeding the baseline, while falling below would count against the claim. (3) The MAP-Elites loop with the two behavioural descriptors evaluates whether exploration covers structural variations and compute-size trade-offs.

schema.problem: Existing AI approaches in scientific discovery act primarily as predictive tools rather than as active collaborators that can generate testable hypotheses, quantify uncertainty, and connect quantum-mechanical predictions with genomic or pharmacogenomic variation across domains.
schema.motivation: An active-collaborator framework could accelerate exploratory discovery across quantum chemistry, catalysis, enzyme kinetics, genomics, and personalized pharmacogenomics by generating new questions and discovery pathways, while reducing reliance on costly quantum calculations and enabling genome-scale variant optimization.
schema.proposed_approach: Three specialized agents—theory, evidence, and consensus—collaboratively generate testable hypotheses, derive governing equations via SymPy-verified symbolic manipulation, optimize multi-objective acquisition functions, and execute virtual experiments with full reproducibility. A quantum-enhanced module implements the standard Bell tunneling correction for parabolic barriers, yielding tunneling probabilities for enzymatic hydrogen-transfer reactions and serving as a DFT-surrogate accelerator. Genomic extensions simulate single-nucleotide polymorphisms that modulate barrier heights, enabling genome-scale enzyme variant optimization. A production-ready, self-contained Python implementation using only NumPy and SciPy is released with embedded data, code, and figures for exact reproducibility.
schema.research_plan: (1) The closed-loop discovery claim is supported by simulation results on benchmark catalyst yield surfaces, quantum-corrected enzyme kinetics, and patient-specific genomic variants, with Sobol-index sensitivity analyses, Bayesian posterior predictive checks, 10-fold cross-validation, and 95% credible intervals. (2) The quantum tunneling prediction claim is evaluated through quantitative tunneling rate enhancement factors at multiple temperatures, calibrated to enzymatic benchmarks with DFT-pluggable barriers, with explicit falsifiability criteria. (3) Reproducibility is assessed by executing the provided kernel with a fixed random seed to regenerate every number, table, plot, and prediction; single-agent BO baselines are used for convergence comparisons.

schema.problem: Automated mathematical reasoning has largely centered on competition mathematics and formal theorem proving, while research-level mathematical problems requiring long-horizon reasoning, literature grounding, and iterative proof refinement remain unaddressed.
schema.motivation: Extending automated reasoning to research-level mathematics would move the field beyond contest-style settings and toward assisting mathematicians with open research problems.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed agentic framework decomposes research-level proof solving into modules for problem analysis, literature search and understanding, fair comparison, knowledge-bank construction, and proof verification. Initializer, proposer, and verifier agents coordinate through a shared structured memory and work in a multi-role, multi-round workflow. Candidate proofs are generated, refined, and verified through iterative feedback; solutions and implementations will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
schema.research_plan: Evidence for the capability claim comes from expert evaluation on a benchmark of ten research-level problems contributed by expert mathematicians across diverse domains. The framework is compared against strong baselines, including GPT-5.2R and Aletheia. Ablation studies isolate the contributions of structured reasoning modules, iterative refinement, and verifier-based feedback; support requires gains that disappear when these components are removed rather than being attributable to a single component. For the comparative claim, failure would occur if expert evaluation did not favor the proposed framework over the baselines.

schema.problem: Autonomous research systems now produce hypotheses faster than they can reliably verify them, so the scarce resource has shifted to bounded compute for verified execution; current greedy implement-to-completion policies waste that budget on verification jobs that die before producing scientific signal.
schema.motivation: Benchmarks indicate that verification is a dominant failure mode and that realistic research-extension tasks are rarely completed, so reallocating finite compute away from unpromising hypotheses can convert otherwise wasted effort into scientific signal.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed scheduling layer treats autonomous discovery as a stochastic, budgeted verification problem. It runs cheap feasibility probes before expensive implementation, then multi-fidelity runs before full-scale confirmation, and uses an index-based abandonment rule to reallocate compute away from unpromising hypotheses.
schema.research_plan: The falsifiable claim is evaluated under a fixed compute budget against greedy sequential verification, round-robin splitting, and ranking-only baselines. The primary evidence is the number of confirmed positive findings per compute unit for each policy, with a separate false-abandonment metric reported to expose the risk of discarding promising hypotheses. The abstract does not specify a concrete experimental environment, dataset, or failure threshold.

schema.problem: Closed-loop AI-scientist systems are currently evaluated only by whether their final reports improve a real baseline, not by whether their discoveries survive when no true effect exists. Because such systems search many hypotheses and select the best result on the same in-sample evidence, they act as multiple-comparison engines, yet no benchmark measures the false-discovery rate of an end-to-end AI scientist and the only paper naming this failure mode documents it qualitatively on two systems.
schema.motivation: Measuring false-discovery rates and auditing discovery claims would let venues reject AI-generated improvements that are false positives; without such control, current multiple-comparison search can produce misleading significant claims and there is no controlled way to detect them.
schema.proposed_approach: Constructs a benchmark of controlled discovery environments by injecting null-effect and weak-effect variants into realistic experimental-design and model-discovery tasks layered on code and data scaffolds from AutoExperiment and EXP-Bench. Each environment includes a hidden ground-truth effect size and a locked confirmation split that is physically absent from the agent's execution sandbox. The benchmark defines a false-discovery rate as the fraction of final significant-improvement claims that fail to reproduce on the confirmation split in null-effect worlds. It is paired with a confirmation protocol that requires the agent to expose its full exploration path, derives an effective number of comparisons from that path, and accepts a final discovery only if it passes a multiplicity-corrected test on the untouched confirmation split; the task suite, scoring harness, and trace-auditing tools are released.
schema.research_plan: (1) The benchmark's hidden ground-truth effect sizes and locked confirmation splits are used to compute the false-discovery rate from final significant-improvement claims in null worlds, testing the hypothesis that current tree-search and iterative agents claim effects in well over 35% of null worlds at a nominal 5% significance convention. (2) The confirmation protocol is evaluated on positive-effect worlds by measuring retention of genuine improvements after deriving an effective number of comparisons and applying a multiplicity-corrected test on the untouched confirmation split; a failure condition would be substantial loss of genuine improvements. (3) The released task suite, scoring harness, and per-agent trace auditing provide the mechanism for venues to run null-world audits.

schema.problem: There is no benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models on research-level Theoretical Computer Science proof generation.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark is built from theorem-proving tasks drawn from papers published at STOC, FOCS, and SODA. Each task provides the necessary context to derive a self-contained proof for a target result. State-of-the-art Large Language Models are evaluated on the benchmark, and generated proofs are checked for correctness by a verification agent; the verifier is further compared against human-expert proof judgments on a set of target statements and generated proof pairs.
schema.research_plan: The evidence for the benchmark's adequacy comes from its construction: tasks are drawn from papers at top TCS venues and designed to provide context for self-contained proofs. State-of-the-art LLMs are evaluated on the benchmark. The correctness of generated proofs is verified by a verification agent, and that verifier is benchmarked against human-expert proof judgments on a set of target statements and generated proof pairs, with expert labels as ground truth.

schema.problem: Automated scientific discovery agents typically test one favored hypothesis and treat failure as a reason to abandon it or move on, rather than maintaining rival mechanistic hypotheses and designing experiments to discriminate between them.
schema.motivation: Mature experimental science progresses through strong inference, where experiments are chosen to discriminate among rival mechanistic hypotheses; closed-loop AI discovery systems now make it possible and valuable to evaluate this kind of experiment-level discriminative competence.
schema.proposed_approach: The proposed protocol requires an AI scientist to (i) co-generate an explicit set of rival mechanism hypotheses, (ii) choose each next experimental condition to maximize the predicted separability of outcomes under those rivals, and (iii) pre-register the predictions of every rival before observing the outcome. The accompanying benchmark provides environments in which pairs of plausible mechanistic models coincide over some query regions but diverge sharply over others, so the central question is whether agents seek out the divergent regions.
schema.research_plan: The paper evaluates the protocol under a fixed query budget in benchmark environments containing pairs of overlapping-but-diverging mechanistic models, comparing recovery of the true generating mechanism and confidence calibration against single-hypothesis falsifiers, parameter-estimation-driven experimental designers, and surprise-driven open-ended explorers. It also probes state-of-the-art LLM agents prompted to test a favored hypothesis for whether they choose discriminating experiments that explicit rivals make easy. The benchmark construction, with models that coincide in some regions and diverge sharply in others, is the evidence for the claim that it isolates experiment-level discriminative power.

schema.problem: It remains unclear whether end-to-end AI materials scientists (dZiner, PriM, MatPilot, DREAMS) and their underlying LLM backbones can reliably discover source-consistent materials knowledge not exposed during training, because existing evaluations occur mostly in low-stakes settings such as simulation of known DFT jobs, language-level hypothesis generation, or self-reported success.
schema.motivation: Recent bottleneck findings that hypothesis feasibility is judged near chance and that plausible yet invalid numbers are reproduced even in guarded pipelines make it timely to close the loop between hypotheses and ground truth and to charge simulation, so that agent failure under domain shift becomes directly measurable.
schema.proposed_approach: The benchmark places end-to-end AI materials agents inside a closed-layer simulator of an archetypal materials property space and queries them for hypotheses, procedures, and queries needed to produce an oracle-simulated number. Answers are scored against deterministic thermodynamic and property databases derived from NIST/ASM/CALPHAD, made unattainable via memorization. Each task is instantiated under both a noiseless and a perturbed oracle, measuring answer accuracy and causal stability under perturbation. Proposed experiments are charged to a finite interaction budget, and agent performance is compared against human-expert baselines.
schema.research_plan: Each task is run under a noiseless and a perturbed oracle, and the causal-stability claim is supported if agents still retrieve the same property law as noise increases beyond the plausible data spread; degradation would indicate failure under domain shift. The costed-simulation grounding charges each proposed experiment against a finite interaction budget; support is rejecting hallucinated values by paying the computational tax, while failure is reproducing plausible-yet-invalid numbers or exceeding the budget through uncosted self-critique. Ground truth is scored against deterministic source-grounded thermodynamic and property databases derived from NIST/ASM/CALPHAD and made unattainable via memorization, so memorization cannot satisfy the tasks. Agent performance is compared against human-expert baselines on the same closed-loop, adversarial-noise tasks, providing the evidence for which failures are agent-specific.
